- ✗ **A. Switch to dynamic first:** membership type and group type are separate settings. Changing how members are added does not unlock the group type.
- ✗ **B. Role-assignable option:** this option can only be set when a group is created, and it is for assigning Microsoft Entra roles. It does not convert one group type into another.
- ✓ **C. New Microsoft 365 group (correct):** the collaboration features belong to the Microsoft 365 group type, and because a group's type is fixed at creation, a new group is the only way to get them.
- ✗ **D. Mail-enable the security group:** a mail-enabled security group only distributes email to its members; it does not provide a shared group mailbox, calendar or group site.

## Key idea
Group type (security or Microsoft 365) is fixed when the group is created; only the membership type can change later.
Q006802:
## Soft delete for users
When a user is deleted in Microsoft Entra ID, the account is not removed at once. It stays in a **suspended (soft-deleted) state for 30 days** and appears on the **Deleted users** page. During that window it can be restored **with all its properties**; the organization information is kept.
After 30 days, permanent deletion starts automatically and can't be stopped. A permanently deleted user can't be restored by anyone, including Microsoft Support; you would have to create a new account and re-enter everything.
## Restoring many users
**Bulk restore** (on the Deleted users page) takes a CSV file whose only required column is `Object ID [objectId]`, one deleted user per row. Errors per row are listed on the Bulk operation results page.
## Licenses after a restore
Licenses that were assigned at the time of deletion are **restored even if none are available**. The tenant can then temporarily use more licenses than it bought, so check license counts afterwards.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Bulk restore with object IDs (correct):** the accounts are still in the 30-day soft-delete window, and Bulk restore takes a CSV of object IDs to bring them back in one job.
- ✗ **B. New object IDs:** a restore brings the same account back with all its properties; that is the reason to restore rather than recreate.
- ✗ **C. Bulk create from the CSV:** this creates brand-new accounts with new IDs and none of the old properties, while the deleted accounts can still simply be restored.
- ✗ **D. Seven-day limit:** the window is 30 days and administrators restore users themselves; after permanent deletion even Microsoft Support can't restore them.
- ✓ **E. Licenses restored (correct):** a restored user gets back the licenses assigned at deletion even when the pool is empty, which can leave the tenant temporarily over its purchased count.

## Key idea
Deleted users stay restorable for 30 days with all their properties (Bulk restore takes object IDs), and their licenses come back even beyond the purchased count.
Q006803:
## Internal accounts versus B2B guests
- An **internal member** is created in your tenant with credentials that your tenant manages. **Bulk create** makes exactly these: its required columns are Name, User name (UPN in one of your domains) and Initial password. It sends **no invitation emails**; you have to hand out the credentials yourself.
- A **B2B collaboration user** is invited by email and signs in with their **own** organization's or identity provider's credentials. The account in your tenant gets user type **Guest** and a UPN like `ana_supplier.com#EXT#@contoso.onmicrosoft.com`.
## Bulk invite
Bulk invite (Users > Bulk operations > Bulk invite) takes a CSV template in which the required values are:
- **Email address to invite**
- **Redirection url**, the page the guest lands on after accepting, such as `https://myapps.microsoft.com`
It can also include a customized invitation message, and invitation emails are sent to the guests.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bulk restore:** restore only brings back users deleted from this tenant within 30 days; it can't import accounts that live in another organization's tenant.
- ✓ **B. Bulk invite (correct):** it creates B2B guest accounts that authenticate with the engineers' own supplier credentials and sends invitation emails, which matches every requirement.
- ✗ **C. Bulk create sends invitations:** bulk create never sends invitations, and it needs a user name in one of the tenant's domains plus an initial password, not an external address.
- ✗ **D. Bulk create with passwords:** this makes internal member accounts with passwords managed by the manufacturer, so the engineers would not use their supplier credentials, and no invitation email is sent.

## Key idea
Bulk create makes internal members with passwords and no emails; bulk invite makes B2B guests who use their own credentials and get an invitation.
Q006804:
## Why licenses need a location
Some Microsoft services aren't available in every country or region. Before a license can be assigned to a user, Microsoft needs the user's **usage location**, a two-letter country or region code such as `DE` or `US`.
## Direct assignment versus group-based licensing
- **Direct assignment**: the administrator must set the user's usage location before the license can be assigned.
- **Group-based licensing**: users without a specific location **inherit the location of the tenant**, so the license can be applied.
That fallback can be wrong for people who work in another country. If users are in several locations, set the usage location as part of user creation (for example, a column in your provisioning process).
## Related error
If a user's usage location is set to a country where a service in the license isn't offered, group-based licensing reports **Usage location isn't allowed**. Fix the location or remove the user from the licensed group.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Owner's location:** the fallback documented by Microsoft is the tenant's location, not the location of a group owner.
- ✗ **B. Location ignored:** group licensing still applies a location (the tenant's), and the "Usage location isn't allowed" error shows that location still matters for group licenses.
- ✗ **C. No location, nearest datacenter:** a license is never applied without a location; the user simply inherits the tenant's location.
- ✓ **D. Tenant location fallback (correct):** group-based licensing fills in the tenant's location for members with no usage location, while a direct assignment requires the administrator to specify one first.

## Key idea
Direct license assignment needs the user's usage location; group-based licensing falls back to the tenant location, so set the correct location when creating users.
Q006805:
## How group-based licensing reports errors
With group-based licensing, licenses are applied in the background as members join. If a license can't be applied, the failure is recorded on the user and shown on the group (a notification lists the users in an error state) and in the admin center's **Errors & issues** view, instead of failing immediately like a direct assignment.
## The "Not enough licenses" error
The group's product has no free licenses left for the extra members. Microsoft's fixes are:
- **buy more licenses** for that product
- **remove unused direct assignments**, for example E5 assigned directly to accounts that no longer need it
- **free licenses** from other groups or users that no longer need them
After fixing the cause, select **Reprocess** for the affected users or group so the assignment is attempted again with the licenses now available.
## Errors that clear by themselves
`LicenseAssignmentAttributeConcurrencyException` in the audit logs comes from several groups assigning the same license at once; it is retried automatically. A shortage of licenses is not like that: nothing changes until licenses are freed or bought.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Buy more licenses (correct):** adding E5 seats to the subscription gives the eight users licenses to take; reprocessing then applies them.
- ✗ **B. Set usage location:** a missing usage location produces a different error, and for group licensing users without one inherit the tenant's location.
- ✗ **C. Reprocess only:** reprocessing retries with the same number of licenses, so the eight users fail again; it helps only after the shortage has been fixed.
- ✗ **D. Convert to dynamic:** membership type doesn't change how many licenses exist; a dynamic group runs into the same shortage.
- ✓ **E. Remove unused direct assignments (correct):** unassigning the 15 direct E5 licenses that nobody uses returns them to the pool, which covers the eight-seat shortfall without buying more.

## Key idea
"Not enough licenses" in group-based licensing is fixed by buying or freeing licenses (such as unused direct assignments) and then reprocessing.
Q006806:
## Conflicting service plans
Each license (product) contains **service plans**, for example Exchange Online (Plan 1) in E1 and Exchange Online (Plan 2) in E3. Some plans can't be assigned to the same user together. When a group tries to give a user a product whose plans conflict with plans the user already has, group-based licensing records a **Conflicting service plans** error for that user.
## How to resolve it
Microsoft lists three fixes:
- remove the redundant **direct** license (here E1, since E3 includes a higher Exchange plan)
- disable one of the conflicting service plans in one of the assignments
- adjust the group license assignment
Then reprocess the user so the group license is applied again.
## Example
After the E1 direct assignment is removed, reprocessing applies E3 from the group, and the user's mailbox moves to the Plan 2 features. The freed E1 license can go to someone else.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Nested group:** group-based licensing doesn't support nested groups, so she would get no E3 at all, and the conflict with E1 would still exist.
- ✗ **B. Usage location:** an unsupported or missing location gives the "Usage location isn't allowed" error, not a plan conflict between Exchange Plan 1 and Plan 2.
- ✗ **C. Buy more licenses:** the error is about two plans clashing on one user, not about a shortage; extra E3 seats would fail for the same reason.
- ✓ **D. Remove the redundant direct license (correct):** once E1 is gone, nothing conflicts with Exchange Online (Plan 2), so the group's E3 can be applied after reprocessing.

## Key idea
A "conflicting service plans" error is fixed by removing the redundant direct license or disabling one of the clashing plans, then reprocessing.
Q006807:
## Group-based licensing and nesting
With group-based licensing, a license assigned to a group is applied to the users who are **members of that group**. It does **not** follow nested groups: if a license is assigned to a group that contains other groups, only the users in the first-level group get the license. The Microsoft Entra documentation lists "applying licenses to nested security groups" among the nesting scenarios that aren't supported.
## How to license the nested users
- Assign E3 directly to the Sales and Support groups as well (one assignment per group), or
- add the users themselves to All-Staff, or
- make All-Staff a dynamic group whose rule includes the right users, for example everyone with `userType = Member`.
## Example
All-Staff has 120 direct user members and two nested groups with 60 users. 120 users show E3; the 60 in Sales and Support show no license and no error, because they were never in scope.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Groups Administrator role:** users never need an admin role to receive a license from a group they are a member of.
- ✓ **B. First-level members only (correct):** licenses assigned to All-Staff are applied to its direct user members; members of nested groups are not processed at all.
- ✗ **C. Dynamic membership required:** membership type doesn't make nested groups count for licensing; group-based licensing ignores nested groups whatever their membership type.
- ✗ **D. 24-hour delay:** nesting isn't delayed, it isn't supported. Waiting won't license the users of Sales and Support.

## Key idea
Group-based licensing applies only to direct members of the licensed group; license the nested groups themselves or add the users directly.
Q006808:
## Licenses follow group membership
With group-based licensing, a user keeps a group's license only while they are a member. When they leave the group, the license is removed; when they join another licensed group, the new license is applied in the background. That processing is not instant: it depends on tenant size and load and can take longer in large tenants.
## Moving users between licensed groups without interruption
Microsoft's documented order is:
- **add** the user to the destination group first
- **confirm** the new license is applied on the user's Licenses page
- **remove** the user from the original group
If the user is removed first, they are unlicensed until the new group's assignment is processed, and services such as the mailbox and Teams become unavailable for that time.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Remove first and wait:** this guarantees a period with no license at all, which is exactly the interruption the user must not have.
- ✗ **B. Same session:** group license processing runs in the background and its timing depends on load; it is not guaranteed to be instant, so the user can be unlicensed in between.
- ✓ **C. Add first, then remove (correct):** while the user is in both groups, the services stay licensed; removing the old group only after the new license is confirmed avoids any gap.
- ✗ **D. Temporary direct assignment:** removing the group first can still leave a gap before the direct license applies, and the extra direct assignment then needs cleanup; adding to the new group first is simpler and safe.

## Key idea
To move a user between licensed groups without losing access, add to the new group, confirm the license, then remove from the old group.
Q006809:
## External collaboration settings
In the Microsoft Entra admin center, **External Identities > External collaboration settings** groups several separate controls:
- **Guest user access**: what guests can see in the directory.
- **Guest invite settings**: **who** in your organization may send invitations.
- **Collaboration restrictions**: **which domains** invitations may be sent to.
## Allow list or block list
Collaboration restrictions work with either an allow list or a block list, never both:
- **Deny invitations to the specified domains**: everything is allowed except the listed domains (common for blocking `gmail.com`, `outlook.com`).
- **Allow invitations only to the specified domains (most restrictive)**: only the listed domains can be invited; every other domain is blocked.
The default is to allow invitations to any domain. Domains are entered one per line, and an invitation to a blocked domain fails with a blocked-domain message.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Allow list (correct):** with "Allow invitations only to the specified domains", only fabrikam.com and litware.com can receive invitations, and every other domain fails automatically.
- ✗ **B. Guest user access:** this limits what guests can see in the directory after they join; it doesn't restrict invitations by domain.
- ✗ **C. Guest invite settings:** this controls which users may invite, not which domains they may invite; there is no domain list in this setting.
- ✗ **D. Block list of personal domains:** a block list stops only the domains listed; invitations to any other company or provider would still be allowed.

## Key idea
To limit B2B invitations to named partners, use Collaboration restrictions with an allow list; a block list only stops the domains listed.
Q006810:
## Who can invite guests
By default, all users, including B2B guests, can invite external users. **Guest invite settings** in External collaboration settings offers four levels:
- **Anyone in the organization can invite guest users including guests and non-admins** (most inclusive)
- **Member users and users assigned to specific admin roles can invite guest users including guests with member permissions**
- **Only users assigned to specific admin roles can invite guest users**: only users with the User Administrator or Guest Inviter role can invite
- **No one in the organization can invite guest users including admins** (most restrictive)
## The Guest Inviter role
**Guest Inviter** lets a user invite guests without giving them a higher-privileged administrator role. Users with this role can invite even when the setting is "Only users assigned to specific admin roles".
## Example
With the admin-roles-only setting, a sales employee's invitation fails, a User Administrator's succeeds, and a project manager with Guest Inviter can invite a consultant but can't reset passwords or edit users.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. User Administrator for managers:** the managers could invite, but they would also be able to create, edit and reset users, which breaks the "no other administrative permissions" requirement.
- ✗ **B. No one can invite:** this blocks User Administrators and the project managers too, so nobody could send the invitations the company still needs.
- ✗ **C. Members and admin roles:** every member user would still be able to invite guests, which is what security wants to stop.
- ✓ **D. Guest Inviter for the managers (correct):** the role grants only the ability to invite guests, so the three managers can invite without any other administrative rights.
- ✓ **E. Admin roles only (correct):** this stops ordinary members and guests from inviting, while User Administrators and Guest Inviters still can.

## Key idea
Restrict invitations with "Only users assigned to specific admin roles" and give non-admins who must invite the Guest Inviter role.
Q006811:
## When the allow or block list is enforced
The B2B collaboration allow or block list is checked when an invitation is sent, together with cross-tenant access settings. Microsoft documents how it treats people who were already invited:
- it **doesn't apply to external users who already redeemed** their invitation
- if an invitation is **pending** and you set a policy that blocks its domain, the user's attempt to **redeem the invitation fails**
- new invitations to the blocked domain fail and the inviter sees a blocked-domain message
## Removing existing access
Because redeemed guests keep their accounts, cutting off a partner needs separate steps: find the guests (filter the Users list for guests, or by domain) and block sign-in, delete them, or remove their group and app assignments.
## Example
After the change, a project manager who tries to invite `lee@rival.example` gets a blocked-domain message, the pending invitee sees redemption fail, and the four existing guests still sign in until an administrator removes them.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Accounts deleted:** the block list never deletes user objects; existing guests must be removed or blocked separately.
- ✓ **B. Redeemed users untouched, pending redemption fails (correct):** the list governs invitations, so it stops the pending one at redemption but doesn't remove or block guests who already accepted.
- ✗ **C. Only at send time:** the block list also affects pending invitations, whose redemption fails once the domain is blocked.
- ✗ **D. Existing blocked, pending allowed:** this is the reverse of the documented behaviour: redeemed guests aren't affected, and a pending invitation to a blocked domain fails at redemption.

## Key idea
A B2B block list stops new and pending invitations but leaves already-redeemed guests in place; remove those users separately.
Q006812:
## Two separate properties of a B2B user
- **Identities** says where the user authenticates, for example `ExternalAzureAD` for a user who signs in with another Microsoft Entra organization's account.
- **User type** says the user's relationship to your organization: `Member` or `Guest`. It doesn't depend on how the user signs in.
Combining them gives four kinds of users: internal member, internal guest, **external guest** (the usual B2B guest) and **external member**, a user who signs in with another organization's account but has member-level access. External members are common in organizations made of several tenants.
## Changing the user type
You can convert User type from Guest to Member (or back) by editing the user's profile in the Microsoft Entra admin center or with PowerShell. Do this only when the relationship really changes, as with an acquired subsidiary. The user keeps authenticating with the home tenant's credentials.
## Default guest permissions
Guests have restricted directory permissions by default: they can manage their own profile but can't read all directory information. Members don't have those limits.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Microsoft 365 group membership:** group membership gives access to the group's resources; it doesn't change a user's directory permissions or user type.
- ✗ **B. New internal accounts:** this would give member access, but the staff would get second credentials managed by the parent, which breaks the requirement to use their subsidiary accounts.
- ✓ **C. Guest to Member (correct):** changing User type gives these users member-level permissions, while their identities stay with the subsidiary tenant, so they keep signing in with their own accounts.
- ✗ **D. Guest user access same as members:** this tenant-wide setting gives every guest, including suppliers and customers, member-level directory access, not only the subsidiary staff.

## Key idea
User type (Member or Guest) is separate from where a user signs in; change a B2B user to Member to give an external user member-level access.
Q006813:
## Scoping SSPR
Self-service password reset (SSPR) can be enabled for **None**, **Selected** or **All** users under **Password reset > Properties**. With **Selected**, the Microsoft Entra admin center currently lets you pick **only one group**.
## Using nested groups
For a wider rollout, SSPR supports **nested groups**: create one group for SSPR, add the department groups to it as members, and select that group. Users in the nested groups are then in scope.
## Example
`SSPR-Enabled` contains the groups `SSPR-Sales` and `SSPR-Support`. Selecting `SSPR-Enabled` puts both teams in scope, and adding a third team later means adding one more group to `SSPR-Enabled`, with no change to the SSPR settings.
## Licensing
Password reset needs at least Microsoft Entra ID P1 (or a Microsoft 365 plan that includes SSPR) for the users who benefit from it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. All users:** "All" brings the whole company into scope, which the requirement excludes; deleting people's authentication methods is not a way to scope SSPR.
- ✓ **B. Parent group with nested groups (correct):** SSPR accepts one selected group and supports nested groups, so a parent group containing both teams puts exactly Sales and Support in scope.
- ✗ **C. Authentication methods policy:** that policy controls which methods a group may register and use; whether users are enabled for SSPR at all is set only by the Password reset scope (None, Selected or All).
- ✗ **D. Second policy:** there is one SSPR configuration for the tenant; you can't create another policy that targets a different group.

## Key idea
SSPR's Selected scope takes one group; put several groups in scope by nesting them in a parent group and selecting that group.
Q006814:
## How SSPR checks a user
When someone starts a reset at `https://aka.ms/sspr`, Microsoft Entra checks that the user is enabled for SSPR and that they have registered **at least as many methods as the policy requires**, out of the methods the administrator enabled. If not, the user is told to contact their administrator.
## Changing the required number
Microsoft documents the effect of raising the requirement from one method to two:
- 1 or more methods registered, 1 required: able to reset
- **1 method registered, 2 required: unable to reset**
- 2 or more registered, 2 required: able to reset
Changing **which** methods are allowed has a similar effect: users whose only registered method was removed from the policy can no longer reset.
## Fix
Ask affected users to register a second method (for example at `https://aka.ms/ssprsetup`), and use the registration settings to prompt users at sign-in. Plan the change and tell users before raising the requirement.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Registration reset:** changing the number of required methods doesn't erase registrations; users with two or more methods can still reset.
- ✗ **B. Synced users disabled:** the number of methods has nothing to do with on-premises passwords; synced users depend on password writeback instead.
- ✓ **C. Only one method registered (correct):** with two methods now required, users who registered just one fail the method check and are sent to their administrator.
- ✗ **D. Admins only:** the number of methods applies to the users in scope; administrators have a separate fixed two-gate policy, so standard users are not excluded.

## Key idea
Raising SSPR's required methods from one to two blocks users who registered only one method until they add another.
Q006815:
## Why synced users can't reset by default
For a user whose password is managed on-premises (federation, pass-through authentication or password hash synchronization), the source of truth is Active Directory Domain Services. SSPR checks for this: **if writeback isn't deployed and the password is managed on-premises, the user is asked to contact their administrator.**
## Password writeback
Writeback sends a password changed or reset in the cloud back to AD DS in real time, where on-premises password policy is checked. It works with password hash sync, pass-through authentication and AD FS. Setting it up takes two switches:
- in the **Microsoft Entra Connect** wizard: Customize synchronization options > **Optional features > Password writeback** (the Connect account also needs Reset password and related permissions in AD DS)
- in the **Microsoft Entra admin center**: **Password reset > On-premises integration > Write back passwords to your on-premises directory**
Writeback uses an Azure Service Bus relay; all traffic is **outbound** over port 443, so no inbound firewall rules are needed.
## Licensing
On-premises writeback requires Microsoft Entra ID P1, P2 or Microsoft 365 Business Premium. Microsoft 365 Business Standard includes cloud SSPR but not writeback.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Writeback in Password reset settings (correct):** SSPR itself must be told to write passwords back to the on-premises directory before synchronized users are allowed to reset.
- ✗ **B. Inbound 443 rule:** writeback communicates through a Service Bus relay with outbound connections only; no inbound rule is required.
- ✗ **C. Business Standard licenses:** those plans don't include on-premises writeback, and the tenant's P1 already covers it.
- ✗ **D. Switch to pass-through authentication:** writeback is supported with password hash synchronization, so changing the sign-in method isn't needed.
- ✓ **E. Writeback in Entra Connect (correct):** the sync server must have the Password writeback feature enabled so it can receive reset requests and set the password in AD DS.

## Key idea
Synced users can use SSPR only after password writeback is enabled both in Microsoft Entra Connect and in the SSPR on-premises integration settings.
Q006816:
## Users must register before they can reset
SSPR can only verify a user with the authentication methods the user has registered, such as the Microsoft Authenticator app, a mobile phone or an email address. A user who has registered nothing can't reset and is told to contact the administrator.
## Registration settings
Under **Password reset > Registration**:
- **Require users to register when signing in = Yes**: users in SSPR scope are prompted to register when they next sign in with a browser or modern authentication (Microsoft 365, the admin center, My Apps, federated and custom apps). They can cancel, but they are prompted at each sign-in until they register.
- **Number of days before users are asked to reconfirm their authentication information**: 0 to 730 days (0 means never). It keeps phone numbers and emails current; this option is available only when registration at sign-in is required.
Without required registration, users are never prompted, though they can still register themselves at `https://aka.ms/ssprsetup`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reset notifications:** this emails users after their password has been reset; it doesn't prompt anyone to register methods beforehand.
- ✗ **B. Custom helpdesk link:** this changes where the "Contact your administrator" link points; it helps users who are already stuck but doesn't make them register.
- ✗ **C. Lower to one method:** a user with zero registered methods still fails the check, because one registered method is still required.
- ✓ **D. Required registration at sign-in (correct):** users are interrupted at their next sign-in until they register methods, so their information is in place before they forget a password; reconfirmation keeps it current.

## Key idea
Turn on "Require users to register when signing in" (with periodic reconfirmation) so users have SSPR methods before they need a reset.
Q006817:
## Two protocols, one per share
Azure Files offers two industry-standard protocols for mounting a share: **SMB** and **NFS** (NFSv4.1). Each share uses one of them. Learn states plainly that a single Azure file share cannot be accessed with both SMB and NFS; you can create an SMB share and a separate NFS share in the same storage account, but they hold separate data.
## Which clients can use which protocol
- **SMB shares** are mounted by Windows (drive letter or UNC path), by Linux through the SMB kernel client (`mount -t cifs`), and by macOS.
- **NFS shares** are for Linux/UNIX workloads that need POSIX semantics, UID/GID permissions and case sensitivity. Learn's NFS page says NFS Azure file shares **aren't supported for Windows**, and lists "access same data from Windows and Linux client" as not supported.
- NFS also needs the SSD (premium) media tier; there is no NFS on HDD.
## Example
A share named `projects` is created as SMB. Windows laptops map it as `P:` and the Ubuntu build server mounts `//<account>.file.core.windows.net/projects` with the SMB client, so everyone works on the same files.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. NFS share for both:** Azure Files NFS shares are not supported on Windows clients, and Linux can also mount SMB, so NFS is neither the only Linux option nor a path for the Windows laptops.
- ✓ **B. SMB share (correct):** SMB is the protocol both client families can use. Windows mounts it natively, and Learn documents mounting SMB Azure file shares on Linux with the SMB kernel client, so one share serves both groups.
- ✗ **C. NFS on HDD:** NFS shares require the SSD media tier, so this configuration cannot be created, and even on SSD the Windows designers could not mount it.
- ✗ **D. SMB and NFS over one data set:** Azure Files does not let one share be accessed with both protocols. Two shares in one account are two separate data sets, so edits in one would never appear in the other.

## Key idea
Mixed Windows and Linux clients on the same files means an SMB share; NFS shares are Linux-only, SSD-only and never shared with SMB.
Q006818:
## How NFS shares decide who may connect
NFS Azure file shares do **not** support user-based authentication: there is no storage account key and no Kerberos/Entra identity in the NFS mount. Instead, Azure Files relies on **network-level access** to decide which clients are allowed. Learn's NFS page states that clients must connect through:
- a **private endpoint**, which gives the share a private IP address in a virtual network (reachable from peered networks and from on-premises over VPN or ExpressRoute), or
- a **service endpoint** with virtual network restrictions on the storage account.
The feature table for NFS shares lists "Grant network access to specific Azure virtual networks" as supported and "Grant network access to specific IP addresses" as **not supported**.
## Example
The firm already has a site-to-site VPN to `vnet-hub`. The admin creates a private endpoint for the `file` sub-resource in that virtual network, makes sure on-premises DNS resolves `<account>.file.core.windows.net` to the private IP, and the server mounts with `mount -t nfs ... -o vers=4,minorversion=1,sec=sys`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Account key in mount options:** NFS shares have no key-based or user-based authentication at all, so there is no key to pass and the IP rule still would not admit the client.
- ✗ **B. Port 445:** TCP 445 is the SMB port. NFS uses its own port, and the failure here is that NFS never trusts an IP rule, not that a port is blocked by the ISP.
- ✗ **C. Identity-based access:** identity-based authentication is listed as not supported for NFS shares; it is an SMB feature, so domain-joining the server changes nothing.
- ✓ **D. No IP rules for NFS (correct):** an IP address firewall rule is not a supported way to admit NFS clients. A private endpoint reached over the existing VPN gives the server a supported, private network path to the share.

## Key idea
NFS Azure file shares trust networks, not identities or IP rules: connect through a private endpoint or a service endpoint from an allowed virtual network.
Q006819:
## Three billing models
Azure Files offers **provisioned v2**, **provisioned v1** and **pay-as-you-go**. Microsoft recommends provisioned v2 for new deployments.
- **Provisioned v2**: you separately provision storage, IOPS and throughput, and you pay for what you provision regardless of usage. The provisioned storage is a hard limit: if you provision 2 TiB and write 2 TiB, the share is full until you raise the size or delete data. You can scale up or down, but a decrease is allowed only after 24 hours have passed since the last increase.
- **Provisioned v1**: you provision storage, and IOPS and throughput follow from it.
- **Pay-as-you-go**: you are billed for used storage, transactions and data transfer. Learn states that this model is **only available for HDD storage**, and pay-as-you-go shares support only SMB.
## Where NFS fits
NFS shares require SSD storage, so they use a provisioned model; there is no pay-as-you-go NFS share.
## Example
A 1 TiB provisioned v2 share holding 200 GiB is billed for 1 TiB plus the provisioned IOPS and throughput. The same data in a pay-as-you-go share is billed for about 200 GiB plus every read and write transaction.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Automatic growth:** the provisioned size is the share's hard limit. When data reaches it, writes fail until an admin increases the provisioned storage or deletes data.
- ✗ **B. Immediate decrease:** provisioned v2 lets you decrease a provisioned quantity only after 24 hours have passed since your last increase, so hourly up-and-down scaling is not possible.
- ✓ **C. Pay-as-you-go is HDD only and usage based (correct):** Learn states the model is only available on HDD and bills for used storage, transactions and data transfer.
- ✗ **D. Pay-as-you-go NFS on SSD:** pay-as-you-go exists only on HDD and supports only SMB, while NFS requires SSD; this combination does not exist.
- ✓ **E. Provisioned v2 bills what you provision (correct):** storage, IOPS and throughput are each provisioned, and that provisioned amount drives the bill, independent of how much the share really uses.

## Key idea
Provisioned v2 = pay for what you provision (storage, IOPS, throughput); pay-as-you-go = HDD-only, SMB-only, pay for usage and transactions.
Q006820:
## Quota versus provisioned size
Every Azure file share has a maximum size it may grow to.
- In **provisioned** shares this value is the **provisioned size**, and you pay for it whether you use it or not.
- In **pay-as-you-go** shares the same setting is called the **quota**. Learn notes that the quota **does not directly affect the bill**: you still pay for the logical data stored and the transactions. If you don't set it, the quota defaults to the maximum the storage account supports.
The share's total logical size is enforced against the quota or provisioned size, so a share can be "full" long before the storage account is.
## What does not count
Learn's snapshot page says share snapshots **don't count towards the maximum share size limit**. Share soft delete works at the level of a whole deleted share, not individual files.
## Example
The share `scans` has a 1 TiB quota and holds 1 TiB of data. The admin raises its quota to 2 TiB in the share's properties; users can save again, and the bill still follows the data actually stored.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Share quota (correct):** the share has reached the maximum size set for it. Raising the quota removes the limit, and in the pay-as-you-go model the quota is only a cap, so a higher value does not raise the bill by itself.
- ✗ **B. Snapshots against quota:** snapshots are differential and are billed, but they don't count towards the share's maximum size, so deleting them frees no room under the quota.
- ✗ **C. Account access tier:** the account default access tier (hot, cool, cold) applies to blob data, not to file share size. Pay-as-you-go file shares have their own tiers (transaction optimized, hot, cool), and none of them changes capacity.
- ✗ **D. Soft delete reserving space:** share soft delete keeps whole deleted shares for the retention period. It doesn't hold space inside a live share for deleted files.

## Key idea
A file share fills up at its own quota or provisioned size, not at the account limit; in pay-as-you-go the quota is a cap, not a charge.
Q006821:
## SMB needs port 445
SMB uses **TCP port 445**. Learn's Windows mount guide says connections fail if 445 is blocked, and recommends `Test-NetConnection -ComputerName <account>.file.core.windows.net -Port 445` to check. Some ISPs and corporate firewalls block outbound traffic on 445.
## Ways around a blocked port
- Open 445 outbound on the firewall, if policy allows.
- Use a **VPN or ExpressRoute** connection so the client reaches the share privately (often through a private endpoint) without exposing 445 to the internet.
Outside the share's Azure region the client must also support **SMB 3.x**, because SMB 2.1 has no encryption and is refused over the public endpoint.
## What does not help
Learn also states that SAS tokens aren't supported for mounting Azure file shares; mounting uses the storage account key or identity-based authentication.
## Example
After a point-to-site VPN to the hub virtual network is set up and the account has a private endpoint, `Test-NetConnection` succeeds against the private IP and the script maps the share as `Z:`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Quota full:** a full quota stops writes on a mounted share. It doesn't make the TCP connection to port 445 fail before any SMB session starts.
- ✗ **B. Switch to NFS:** NFS Azure file shares aren't supported on Windows clients, and NFS shares need a private endpoint or service endpoint rather than internet access.
- ✗ **C. SAS token for the mount:** SAS tokens aren't supported for mounting Azure file shares, and authentication is never reached anyway because the TCP connection itself fails.
- ✓ **D. Blocked port 445 (correct):** the failed TCP test is the classic symptom of an ISP or firewall dropping 445. A VPN or ExpressRoute connection is the documented way to mount from outside Azure without opening that port.

## Key idea
When an SMB mount fails and the port 445 test fails, the network blocks SMB: open 445 or route the traffic over VPN or ExpressRoute.
Q006822:
## Where anonymous access is configured
Anonymous (public) read access to blob data is controlled by two settings:
- **Storage account**: *Allow Blob anonymous access* (`AllowBlobPublicAccess`). If it is disabled, no container can be anonymous. In this scenario it is already enabled.
- **Container**: the anonymous access level. Learn states that you **can't change the anonymous access level for an individual blob**; it is set **only at the container level** and applies to every blob in that container.
Because blob storage has a flat namespace, `drafts/` is just part of each blob's name, not a separate object that carries its own access level.
## The three container levels
- **Private** (default): every request must be authorized.
- **Blob**: anonymous clients can read any blob in the container if they know its URL, but can't enumerate the blobs.
- **Container**: anonymous clients can read blobs and also list the blobs in the container (but never list the account's containers).
## Example
The admin copies `media/drafts/*` into a new Private container `media-drafts` (for example with AzCopy), deletes the originals, and sets `media` to **Blob**. `https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/media/vase.jpg` loads in a browser, while listing `media` or reading anything in `media-drafts` fails for anonymous callers.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Private level on a virtual directory:** the anonymous access level exists only on containers. A prefix such as `drafts/` is part of the blob names and can't carry its own access level.
- ✓ **B. Separate container, then Blob level (correct):** the access level always covers a whole container, so blobs that must stay private have to live in a different, Private container. The Blob level then serves the public images by URL without letting visitors list them.
- ✗ **C. Random draft names:** with the Blob level every blob in `media` is readable by anyone who has its URL. Hard-to-guess names hide the drafts but don't stop anonymous reads once a URL leaks.
- ✗ **D. Container level:** this level lets anonymous clients enumerate the blobs in the container, so visitors could list every image, including the drafts.

## Key idea
Anonymous access is set per container, never per blob or folder: keep private blobs in a Private container and use Blob (read by URL, no listing) for public ones.
Q006823:
## Default access tier
Every general-purpose v2 account has a **default access tier**: hot (the default for new accounts), cool or cold. It decides the online tier of a new blob when the upload doesn't specify one. **Archive can't be the default access tier.**
## Inferred versus explicit tiers
- A blob uploaded without a tier has an **inferred** tier: it follows the account default, and the portal shows *Hot (inferred)*, *Cool (inferred)* or *Cold (inferred)*.
- A blob whose tier was set on upload or later with Set Blob Tier has an **explicit** tier, which the account default no longer affects.
Learn states that changing the default access tier **applies to all blobs for which an access tier hasn't been explicitly set**.
## What the change costs
- Toggling the default to a **cooler** tier in a general-purpose v2 account is charged as **write operations** (per 10,000) for every blob with an inferred tier.
- Toggling to a **warmer** tier is charged as **read operations** (per 10,000) plus **data retrieval** (per GB) for those blobs.
## Example
After the change, the 5,000 inferred blobs show *Cool (inferred)* and the bill shows write operations for them; the 200 blobs still show *Hot*. To move those too, the admin would run Set Blob Tier on them or use a lifecycle rule.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Inferred blobs follow the default (correct):** changing the default access tier re-tiers every blob without an explicit tier, and moving to a cooler tier in a general-purpose v2 account is billed as write operations for those blobs. Explicitly tiered blobs keep their tier.
- ✗ **B. No charge:** in a general-purpose v2 account the switch to a cooler default is charged as write operations for every inferred blob, so large containers can make the change noticeably costly.
- ✗ **C. Only new uploads affected:** inferred blobs have no tier of their own, so they move with the account default as soon as it changes, not only blobs uploaded afterwards.
- ✗ **D. Default overrides explicit tiers:** the default only applies to blobs whose tier is inferred. A tier set explicitly on a blob stays until someone changes that blob's tier.

## Key idea
Changing the account default tier moves every blob with an inferred tier (billed as tier-change operations) and leaves explicitly tiered blobs where they are.
Q006824:
## Rehydrating from archive
A blob in the **archive** tier is offline: it cannot be read or modified until it is **rehydrated** to hot, cool or cold, either with **Set Blob Tier** on the blob itself or with **Copy Blob** to a new online blob.
## Rehydration priority
- **Standard** (default): processed in the order received; can take up to 15 hours for objects under 10 GB.
- **High**: prioritized; may finish in under an hour for objects under 10 GB, at a higher cost.
While a standard request is pending, you **can raise** a blob's priority to High (for example, bulk restore at Standard and then expedite the few urgent blobs). You **can't lower** a pending request from High to Standard, and a Set Blob Tier request **can't be cancelled** once it starts. High-priority throughput is also limited per storage account, so expedite only what is urgent.
## Example
`az storage blob set-tier --container-name contracts --name 2021/acme.pdf --tier Hot --rehydrate-priority High` updates the pending request for that blob (the target tier must match the one in the original request); the other 399 blobs continue at Standard.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cancel and restart:** a Set Blob Tier request can't be cancelled after it starts. The supported path is to update the priority of the pending request.
- ✗ **B. Snapshot of an archived blob:** snapshots aren't supported for archived blobs, and a snapshot would still not make offline data readable.
- ✓ **C. Raise priority to High (correct):** Learn explicitly allows updating a pending standard-priority rehydration to High for individual blobs that are needed sooner, without touching the rest of the bulk job.
- ✗ **D. AzCopy download from archive:** no tool can read archived blob data; only metadata and properties are available until rehydration completes.

## Key idea
A pending standard rehydration can be raised to High priority for urgent blobs; it can't be cancelled or lowered from High to Standard.
Q006825:
## Why rehydrated blobs get re-archived
A lifecycle rule checks each blob's age against a time condition. Learn points out that **changing a blob's tier does not change its last modified time** (nor its last access time). After rehydration, a blob modified three years ago still matches `daysAfterModificationGreaterThan: 180`, so a later policy run archives it again.
## Two documented fixes
- Add `daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan` to the `tierToArchive` action. It sets the minimum number of days a rehydrated blob stays online before the rule may archive it again, and it applies only to `tierToArchive`.
- Rehydrate by **Copy Blob** to a new blob in an online tier. The copy is a new blob with a new last modified time, so the rule doesn't match it, and the archived source stays untouched.
## Example
```
"tierToArchive": { "daysAfterModificationGreaterThan": 180,
"daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan": 30 }
```

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Enable versioning:** rehydration doesn't write the blob, so no new version is created, and lifecycle rules for the current version still use its old last modified time.
- ✗ **B. Auto tier to hot:** `enableAutoTierToHotFromCool` only moves cool blobs back to hot when accessed, works with the last access condition, and does nothing to stop a `tierToArchive` action.
- ✗ **C. Creation time reset:** a tier change works on the existing blob and doesn't create a new one, so its creation time stays three years old. The blob would still match a 180-day creation condition and be archived again.
- ✓ **D. Tier-change condition or copy (correct):** the extra condition keeps any rehydrated blob online for the chosen period, and copying creates a fresh blob with a new modified time; both are the remedies Learn gives for this exact behaviour.

## Key idea
Changing a blob's tier keeps its last modified time; use `daysAfterLastTierChangeGreaterThan` (or rehydrate by copy) so lifecycle rules don't re-archive rehydrated blobs.
Q006826:
## How lifecycle filters select blobs
A lifecycle rule has **filters** (which blobs), **conditions** (how old) and **actions** (what to do).
- `blobTypes` is required: `blockBlob` or `appendBlob`.
- `prefixMatch` is optional, up to 10 case-sensitive prefixes per rule. Learn states that **a prefix string must start with a container name**: to match `https://<account>.blob.core.windows.net/sample-container/blob1/...` you write `sample-container/blob1`.
- Prefixes don't support wildcards; `*` and `?` are treated as literal characters.
- `blobIndexMatch` (blob index tags) is optional. If several filters are set they are combined with AND, and filters can only include blobs, never exclude them.
## Timing
After you add or change rules, it can take up to 24 hours before the changes take effect and the first run starts; after that the policy runs periodically and evaluates each blob once per run.
## Example
```
"filters": { "blobTypes": ["blockBlob"], "prefixMatch": ["app/logs/"] },
"actions": { "baseBlob": { "delete": { "daysAfterModificationGreaterThan": 90 } } }
```

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Container name in the prefix (correct):** `logs/` would match only blobs in a container literally named `logs`. Writing `app/logs/` matches the log blobs inside container `app`.
- ✗ **B. Index tag filter required:** `blobIndexMatch` is optional. A rule can filter on prefix alone, or even on no prefix at all to cover the whole account.
- ✗ **C. Wildcard:** prefix strings don't support wildcard matching; `logs/*` would look for names that literally contain an asterisk and match nothing.
- ✗ **D. 30 days to start:** rule changes take up to 24 hours to take effect, and the rule was created a week ago, so timing is not the reason.

## Key idea
Lifecycle `prefixMatch` values start with the container name (`container/path`) and don't support wildcards.
Q006827:
## Lifecycle conditions
Lifecycle conditions are based on three blob times:
- `daysAfterCreationGreaterThan`: creation time
- `daysAfterModificationGreaterThan`: last write
- `daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan`: last **read or write**, available only when **access time tracking** is enabled on the account
## Last access time
With tracking on, the blob property `LastAccessTime` is updated by access operations such as Get Blob and Put Blob (at most once per 24 hours per blob). Get Blob Properties, Get Blob Metadata and Get Blob Tags don't count as access. If tracking is off, the rule uses the date tracking was enabled instead of real access times, so it can't follow reads.
## Moving back to hot
`enableAutoTierToHotFromCool` moves a cool blob back to hot when it is accessed. It works only together with `daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan`, has no effect on blobs that were already in cool before the action was enabled in a rule, and moves a blob back at most once in 30 days to avoid repeated early deletion charges.
## Example
`az storage account blob-service-properties update --enable-last-access-tracking true`, then a rule with `"tierToCool": {"daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan": 60}, "enableAutoTierToHotFromCool": true`.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cool as the default tier:** changing the default re-tiers every inferred blob at once, regardless of how often each image is read, and nothing ever moves a read image back to hot.
- ✓ **B. Last access condition with auto tier (correct):** this rule cools images that haven't been read for 60 days, and the auto tier flag returns an image to hot as soon as it is accessed again.
- ✗ **C. Modification-based condition:** images are written once and then only read, so modification time ignores reads; `enableAutoTierToHotFromCool` is also only available with the last access condition.
- ✗ **D. Versioning:** versions are created by writes, not reads, and they play no part in tracking access; this only adds storage cost.
- ✓ **E. Access time tracking (correct):** without it the account doesn't record reads, so "not read for 60 days" can't be evaluated and the last access condition falls back to the date tracking was enabled.

## Key idea
To tier by reads, enable access time tracking and use `daysAfterLastAccessTimeGreaterThan`; add `enableAutoTierToHotFromCool` to bring accessed blobs back to hot.
Q006828:
## What a delete does when versioning is on
With **blob versioning** enabled, deleting a blob does not remove its data: the **current version becomes a previous version**, and the blob has no current version any more. Earlier previous versions persist too.
**Blob soft delete** adds a safety net for versions and snapshots that are deleted explicitly: they are kept for the retention period (1 to 365 days).
## Restoring
Learn's soft delete management page explains the difference:
- **Versioning disabled**: Undelete restores the soft-deleted blob and its snapshots.
- **Versioning enabled**: Undelete restores soft-deleted **versions or snapshots**, but **does not restore the base blob**. To get the blob back, **promote a previous version** to be the current version (portal: Versions tab > *Make current version*; in code, copy the version over the base blob).
## Example
The Versions tab of `budget.xlsx` lists the version from yesterday 16:02. Make current version copies it to the base blob, which is then current again; the older versions stay available.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Wait for retention:** when the retention period ends, soft-deleted data is permanently deleted, not restored. Waiting would only risk losing data.
- ✗ **B. Disable versioning first:** disabling versioning doesn't change how the existing deletion was recorded; the data is still a previous version that must be promoted.
- ✓ **C. Promote a previous version (correct):** when versioning is enabled the deleted blob's data lives on as a previous version, and promoting it is the documented way to restore the base blob.
- ✗ **D. Restore Container:** Restore Container applies only to a soft-deleted container. Here the container was never deleted, only one blob.

## Key idea
With versioning on, a deleted blob is restored by promoting a previous version; Undelete alone brings back versions and snapshots, not the base blob.
Q006829:
## How container soft delete works
When **container soft delete** is enabled, a deleted container and its contents are kept for the retention period (1 to 365 days, default 7). During that time **Restore Container** brings back the container with its blobs, versions and snapshots.
## Rules that trip admins up
- A container can be restored **only to its original name**. If a new container with that name exists, you must rename or delete it before restoring.
- Changing the retention period applies only to containers deleted after the change.
- Container soft delete restores whole containers; a single blob deleted from a live container needs **blob soft delete** or **versioning**.
- Blob soft delete and container soft delete have independent retention periods; align them so a restored container isn't missing blobs.
- The least privileged built-in role for restoring a container is **Storage Blob Data Contributor**.
## Example
The admin deletes the empty new `invoices` container, enables *Show deleted containers*, selects the soft-deleted `invoices` and chooses Undelete; all invoice blobs reappear.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Undelete each blob:** Restore Container brings back the container together with its blobs, versions and snapshots. Blob soft delete protects individual blobs, not a deleted container, so per-blob undelete is not the tool here.
- ✓ **B. Clear the name, then restore (correct):** the soft-deleted container can only come back as `invoices`, and the new container is occupying that name, so it has to be removed first.
- ✗ **C. Raise the retention:** a new retention period applies only to containers deleted after the change, and the container is well within its 30 days already.
- ✗ **D. Restore under a new name:** container soft delete doesn't restore to a different name; Learn states a container must be restored to its original name.

## Key idea
A soft-deleted container restores only to its original name, so any new container with that name must be deleted or renamed first.
Q006830:
## Share snapshots
A **share snapshot** is a read-only, point-in-time, incremental copy of an Azure file share. You can browse it and **restore individual files or folders** by copying them back to the live share or to another location. On Windows, SMB share snapshots appear in File Explorer's **Previous Versions** tab, and Robocopy can copy from the snapshot path. A share keeps up to 200 snapshots; Azure Backup can schedule them.
## Share soft delete
**Soft delete for file shares** works **only at the share level**: it protects against deleting the whole share and restores it, with its snapshots, during the retention period. Learn says that to restore deleted files you use share snapshots or Azure file share backup.
## Important detail
Snapshots are deleted together with the share; you can't delete a share and keep its snapshots. Soft delete covers that case by bringing back the share and its snapshots.
## Example
In File Explorer on the mapped drive, the admin opens Properties > Previous Versions on the share root, picks last night's snapshot, and copies `Contracts` back.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Promote the snapshot to the base share:** snapshots aren't promoted to the base share. Restoring is done by copying data out, and the whole-share revert that exists for SMB is only a limited preview.
- ✗ **B. Share soft delete for a folder:** share soft delete only restores entire deleted shares; Learn says to use share snapshots or Azure file share backup to restore deleted files.
- ✗ **C. Point-in-time restore:** point-in-time restore is a Blob Storage feature for block blobs. It doesn't roll back Azure file shares.
- ✓ **D. Copy from the snapshot (correct):** the nightly snapshot holds the folder as of last night, and item-level restore by copying (via Previous Versions or the snapshot path) is how Azure Files recovers deleted files and folders.

## Key idea
Deleted files or folders in an Azure file share come back from share snapshots; share soft delete only restores a deleted share.
Q006831:
## Snapshots live and die with their share
Learn's share snapshot page is explicit: snapshots persist until you delete them or **until the file share is deleted**. You **can't delete a file share and keep its snapshots**; the delete workflow removes them automatically.
## Share soft delete to the rescue
**Soft delete for Azure file shares** is set at the storage account level (on by default for new accounts, retention 1 to 365 days, default 7). A deleted share stays in a soft-deleted state for the retention period, and **undelete restores the share and all its contents, including snapshots**, to their state before deletion.
## How to restore
- Portal: File shares > enable *Show deleted shares* > select the share > Undelete.
- CLI: `az storage share-rm list --include-deleted` to find the deleted version, then `az storage share-rm restore --name <share> --deleted-version <version>`.
## Lesson for the future
To keep historical data from a share you plan to remove, copy the needed files out first (for example with AzCopy) or keep the share; snapshots cannot outlive it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Recreate a share with the same name:** a new share is a new, empty share with no snapshots, and nothing reconnects old snapshots to it.
- ✗ **B. Undelete Blob:** Azure Files share snapshots are not blob snapshots, and Undelete Blob is a Blob Storage operation that has no effect on file shares.
- ✓ **C. Undelete the share (correct):** share soft delete keeps the whole deleted share, snapshots included, and undeleting it within 14 days brings back all 20 snapshots unchanged.
- ✗ **D. Account snapshot list:** snapshots are not kept separately after their share is deleted; they are part of the soft-deleted share and come back only when the share is undeleted.

## Key idea
Deleting an Azure file share deletes its snapshots; share soft delete is what restores the share and its snapshots within the retention period.
Q006832:
## Versions versus snapshots
- A **blob version** is automatic and system-managed. With versioning enabled, every write (Put Blob, Put Block List, Copy Blob) and every **Set Blob Metadata** creates a new version; the old state becomes a previous version with its own version ID. No application change is needed.
- A **blob snapshot** is manual: an application or admin explicitly creates a point-in-time copy, for example before a planned update. Learn recommends stopping block blob snapshots once versioning is on.
## What blob soft delete covers
Blob soft delete keeps deleted blobs, and on overwrite creates a soft-deleted snapshot of the old data. But Learn states that soft delete **doesn't protect against writes to blob metadata or properties**; it points to versioning for that.
## Rolling back
To roll back, promote a previous version: copy it over the base blob (portal: *Make current version*). Microsoft recommends combining versioning with blob soft delete and container soft delete, and using a lifecycle rule to delete old versions to control cost.
## Example
`az storage account blob-service-properties update --resource-group rg-claims --account-name stclaims --enable-versioning true`

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Blob versioning (correct):** it captures the prior state on every overwrite and on metadata updates with no change to the job, and any previous version can be promoted to roll the blob back.
- ✗ **B. Container soft delete:** it only restores a whole deleted container. It records nothing about overwrites of blobs in a container that still exists.
- ✗ **C. Blob soft delete:** it protects deletes and overwrites, but Learn says it doesn't protect metadata or property updates, so metadata changes by the job would be lost.
- ✗ **D. Automatic snapshots:** snapshots are manual and application-driven; Azure doesn't take them on each write, so the job would have to be changed to create them.

## Key idea
For automatic protection of every overwrite and metadata change, enable blob versioning; snapshots are manual and soft delete misses metadata updates.
Q006833:
## Hosting a domain in Azure DNS takes two steps
Creating a zone in Azure DNS only stores records on Azure's authoritative name servers. Nobody on the internet asks those servers anything until the parent zone (here `.com`) says that Azure's name servers are responsible for the domain.
- **Step 1, create the zone**: Azure assigns four name servers from a pool, for example `ns1-37.azure-dns.com`, `ns2-37.azure-dns.net`, `ns3-37.azure-dns.org` and `ns4-37.azure-dns.info`, and creates the authoritative NS record set at the apex automatically.
- **Step 2, delegate**: at the registrar you set the domain's NS records to those Azure name servers. The registrar stores them in the parent zone. This is called delegation.
## How resolution finds the zone
A recursive resolver starts at the root, asks the `.com` servers which name servers host `fabrikam-shop.com`, and then queries those servers. If `.com` still lists the old provider, the old provider's answers win, no matter what the Azure zone contains.
## Checking the result
Microsoft recommends using all four Azure name servers and verifying with `nslookup -type=SOA fabrikam-shop.com`: the primary name server in the answer should be an Azure DNS server. Allow time for caches to expire after the change.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Transfer registration to Azure DNS:** Azure DNS hosts zones but doesn't sell or register domain names; Learn says to buy domains from a third-party registrar. You keep the registration where it is and delegate the domain to Azure DNS.
- ✗ **B. Add registrar servers to the apex NS:** extra servers in the Azure zone's own NS record set are for co-hosting a zone with another provider. They change nothing in the `.com` parent, which still delegates to the old provider.
- ✗ **C. A record for the name server:** an A record maps a host name to an address for clients to connect to; it does not tell resolvers which servers are authoritative for the domain. Only NS records in the parent zone do that.
- ✓ **D. Delegate at the registrar (correct):** the parent `.com` zone learns the Azure name servers only through the registrar, so updating the NS records there (all four servers, copied with their trailing period where the registrar needs it) is what sends internet queries to the Azure zone.

## Key idea
A public Azure DNS zone answers internet queries only after the registrar's NS records for the domain point to the zone's four Azure name servers.
Q006834:
## Child zones are delegated by the parent zone
DNS is a hierarchy of zones. A subdomain can live in the same zone as its parent (just records named `dev` or `api.dev`), or in its own **child zone**. A child zone is invisible until the parent zone contains an **NS record set with the child's name** that lists the child zone's name servers.
## What happens in this scenario
- Resolvers find `contoso.com` in Azure DNS through the registrar delegation.
- They ask the `contoso.com` zone about `api.dev.contoso.com`. That zone has no record named `api.dev` and no NS record for `dev`, so it answers NXDOMAIN.
- The `dev.contoso.com` zone exists, with its own four name servers, but nothing points to it.
## Fixing it
Look up the four name servers on the child zone's Overview page and create an NS record set `dev` in the parent zone with those values. ## Two problems at the zone apex
The apex (relative name `@`) is the zone name itself, `tailspin.com`. Two rules make it special:
- **No CNAME at the apex**: every zone has NS and SOA record sets at `@`, and the DNS standard forbids a CNAME next to other record sets with the same name. So you cannot "point" the bare domain at another host name with a CNAME.
- **Dangling records**: a normal A record holds a fixed address. If the public IP resource is deleted and Azure later hands that address to someone else, users would be sent to a stranger's service.
## Alias record sets
An Azure DNS **alias record set** is an A, AAAA or CNAME record set that references an Azure resource instead of literal data. Supported targets include a Standard public IP address, a Traffic Manager profile, an Azure CDN endpoint, an Azure Front Door endpoint and another record set in the same zone.
- The record set updates automatically when the referenced public IP address changes.
- If the referenced resource is deleted, the alias becomes an empty record set instead of a stale address.
- Alias A/AAAA record sets can be created at the zone apex.
In the portal you add a record set, choose **Alias record set: Yes**, alias type **Azure resource**, and pick the public IP.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Alias A record at the apex (correct):** it is allowed at `@`, resolves to the current address of the Standard public IP, and turns into an empty record set if that resource is deleted, which prevents a dangling record.
- ✗ **B. NS record at the apex:** NS records name authoritative DNS servers. A load balancer frontend is not a DNS server, and the apex NS record set's Azure name servers cannot be replaced anyway.
- ✗ **C. Plain A record with a short TTL:** a short TTL only makes clients re-query sooner; the record itself still returns the old address after `pip-shop` is deleted until someone edits it by hand.
- ✗ **D. CNAME at the apex:** Azure DNS rejects it because the apex already holds the NS and SOA record sets, and a CNAME cannot coexist with other record sets of the same name.

## Key idea
Point the zone apex at an Azure resource with an alias record set; it is allowed at `@` and tracks the resource so records never dangle.
Q006836:
## Record sets in Azure DNS
Azure DNS manages records as **record sets**: all records in a zone with the same name and the same type. If `www` must return two IPv4 addresses, you add a second record to the existing `www` A record set rather than creating another record set.
## Rules worth knowing
- **TTL per record set**: the TTL is a property of the record set, so all records in it share the value.
- **CNAME limits**: a CNAME record set holds a single record and cannot coexist with other record sets of the same name. Because the apex always has NS and SOA record sets, a CNAME at `@` is impossible (use an alias record set instead).
- **Apex NS record set**: created and deleted with the zone. You can add name servers (to co-host with another provider) and change its TTL, but you cannot remove or modify the prepopulated Azure name servers. Other NS record sets, used for delegating child zones, can be changed freely.
- **Wildcards**: the name `*` (or `*.foo`) is supported for all record types except NS and SOA.
- **SOA**: created automatically; the serial number is not incremented automatically when records change.
## Example
`www  3600  A  203.0.113.10` and `www  3600  A  203.0.113.11` are one record set with one TTL of 3600 seconds.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Replace the apex NS servers:** you may add extra name servers to the apex NS record set and change its TTL, but removing or modifying the prepopulated Azure DNS name servers is not allowed.
- ✗ **B. Two `www` A record sets:** a record set is defined by name plus type, so all A records named `www` belong to one record set and share a single TTL.
- ✓ **C. No CNAME at the apex (correct):** the NS and SOA record sets exist at `@` from the moment the zone is created, and a CNAME cannot share its name with any other record set.
- ✗ **D. Wildcard NS record set:** Azure DNS supports wildcard record sets for every record type except NS and SOA, so delegation always uses named NS record sets.
- ✓ **E. TTL on the record set (correct):** Azure DNS specifies the TTL for the record set, not for each record, so all records in the set share it.

## Key idea
In Azure DNS the record set (name plus type) is the unit you manage: one TTL per set, no CNAME at the apex, no wildcard NS, and the Azure apex name servers stay.

## Where autoregistered records come from
With autoregistration enabled on a virtual network link, Azure DNS keeps an A record for each VM in the zone. The data comes from the **Azure DHCP service**, that is, from the IP configuration of the VM's network interface in Azure:
- The record is updated when the VM's IP address changes in Azure, and removed when the VM is deleted or stopped (deallocated).
- Registration messages sent by the guest OS are ignored. Learn's FAQ: if you disable DHCP in the VM and configure a static IP or a new host name inside the OS, the change is not reflected in the zone.
## Static private IPs belong on the NIC
A VM's private address is assigned to its Azure network interface. Learn advises against setting the private IP inside the operating system; if you do, it must match the address on the Azure NIC, otherwise the VM can lose connectivity.
To keep an address fixed, change the NIC's IP configuration from **Dynamic** to **Static** and enter the address (for example `10.4.0.50`, an unused address in the subnet). The guest keeps using DHCP and receives that address.
## Disabling autoregistration is not a refresh
Disabling autoregistration on a link immediately deletes every record registered through that link; re-enabling it registers the addresses that Azure DHCP hands out, not what is typed in the guest.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. `ipconfig /registerdns`:** private zone records are populated by the Azure DHCP service and client registration messages are ignored, so the dynamic update has no effect. The address mismatch also remains.
- ✗ **B. Disable and re-enable autoregistration:** disabling it deletes all records registered through the link, and re-enabling registers the address Azure DHCP assigns (`10.4.0.4`), not the one typed in Windows. The VM stays unreachable.
- ✓ **C. Static IP on the Azure NIC, DHCP in the guest (correct):** the NIC then carries `10.4.0.50`, Windows receives it by DHCP so connectivity returns, and autoregistration updates the `app01` record because the VM's IP changed in Azure.
- ✗ **D. Manual A record:** a manual record does overwrite the autoregistered one, but the NIC in Azure still owns `10.4.0.4`, so the guest's `10.4.0.50` does not match and the VM stays unreachable at either address.

## Key idea
Autoregistration follows the IP configured on the Azure NIC through Azure DHCP; set static private IPs on the NIC, never only inside the guest OS.

## Who answers a VM's DNS query?
Each VNet (or NIC) has a DNS server setting.
- **Azure-provided DNS** (default): VMs send queries to the virtual IP `168.63.129.16`. That resolver knows the private DNS zones linked to the VNet.
- **Custom DNS servers** (here two domain controllers): VMs send every query to those servers. A custom DNS setting at the VNet or NIC level takes precedence over the linked private zone, so the zone is only used if the custom server itself asks Azure DNS.
## Making custom DNS servers see a private zone
The domain controllers run inside `vnet-prod`, which is linked to the zone. If they forward queries for `apps.contoso.net` to `168.63.129.16`, Azure DNS answers from the linked private zone. A conditional forwarder (or a general forwarder to `168.63.129.16`) is the usual design: the DCs answer their Active Directory zones and pass everything else to Azure.
## Symptom to recognise
`nslookup` shows the custom server (`10.20.0.4`) as the server and returns NXDOMAIN: the DC does not host the zone and has nowhere to send the query.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Enable autoregistration:** autoregistration only creates A records for VMs in the linked VNet. The clients still send their queries to the DCs, which never consult the private zone.
- ✗ **B. Second link to the same VNet:** Azure allows only one link between a private DNS zone and a given virtual network, and a link does not change which server VMs query.
- ✗ **C. Public NS record to the DCs:** public NS records serve internet resolvers. They have no effect on how the DCs inside the VNet resolve a name they do not host, and would publish private addresses.
- ✓ **D. Conditional forwarder to `168.63.129.16` (correct):** the DCs sit in a VNet that is linked to the zone, so forwarding the zone's queries to the Azure recursive resolver returns the private zone's records to every client that uses the DCs.

## Key idea
With custom DNS servers on a VNet, private DNS zones work only if those servers forward the zone's queries to `168.63.129.16` from a linked VNet.
